title: THE GOSPEL THAT PROMISES YOU EVERYTHING—EXCEPT THE CROSS
paragraphs: THE GOSPEL THAT PROMISES YOU EVERYTHING—EXCEPT THE CROSS
Is the Prosperity Gospel Simply Misunderstood Scripture, or Has It Become the Very Different Gospel the Apostle Paul Warned Us About?
There is a kind of preaching that can make a struggling person feel like heaven is finally about to open.
The mother who has been praying over unpaid bills hears that her financial breakthrough is coming.
The father who has been unemployed for months is told that his season of supernatural abundance is just around the corner.
The woman fighting cancer hears that if she believes strongly enough, healing is guaranteed.
The young believer who has given everything he can afford is promised that God will multiply his offering a hundredfold.
And for one beautiful moment, everyone feels hopeful.
Then the bills remain unpaid.
The cancer progresses.
The job never comes.
The promised breakthrough doesn't arrive.
And the same person who was told that faith would change everything begins wondering whether the problem is not the preacher, not the promise, not the interpretation of Scripture...
But himself.
Maybe I didn't believe enough.
Maybe I didn't give enough.
Maybe God is disappointed in me.
And somewhere in that terrible silence, a wounded Christian begins confusing unanswered expectations with the absence of God's love.
That is where this conversation becomes more than a theological disagreement.
Because when someone changes what God has promised, people can end up blaming themselves for promises God never made.
And the question we must face is not whether God can bless His children financially.
Of course He can.
The question is far more serious.

When wealth becomes evidence of God's favor, poverty becomes evidence of spiritual failure, and giving becomes a transaction to secure divine rewards, are we still preaching the Gospel Jesus Christ gave His Church?
Or have we placed the name of Jesus over a message that He never taught?
Stay with me, because the answer is not as simple as condemning every wealthy Christian or criticizing every church that speaks about blessings.
Scripture is more beautiful, more demanding, and far more liberating than either extreme.
And there is something about the cross that exposes the entire issue.
Something we cannot afford to miss.
The apostle Paul once wrote words so severe that they should make every preacher, ministry leader, and Christian content creator examine the message they proclaim.

In Galatians 1:6–9, Paul expressed astonishment that believers were turning toward a different gospel. He warned that even if an angel from heaven proclaimed a gospel contrary to the one the apostles had preached, that message was to be rejected.
The Greek wording matters.
Paul used the expression ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον (heteron euangelion), meaning "a different gospel."
He immediately clarified that it was not truly another gospel at all.
His concern was not that Christians disagreed about secondary matters.
His concern was that people were distorting the message of Christ.

In its original context, Galatians confronted teachers who were making observance of the Mosaic Law, particularly circumcision, necessary for full inclusion among God's covenant people. Paul defended justification through faith in Jesus Christ rather than through works of the Law.
That historical context must not be erased.
Paul was not specifically writing about modern prosperity preaching.
But his warning establishes a principle that reaches far beyond first-century Galatia.
When something other than the saving work of Jesus Christ becomes essential to the message of salvation, the Gospel itself is being altered.
And when the Gospel is altered, the consequences are eternal.
So what exactly is the prosperity gospel?
We need to be careful here, because not every sermon about God's provision is prosperity theology.
Not every Christian who becomes financially successful has compromised the faith.
Not every prayer for healing is an expression of unbelief or greed.
And not every preacher who encourages generosity is exploiting people.
The Bible openly acknowledges that material blessings can come from God.

Abraham possessed great wealth. Job experienced prosperity before his suffering and restoration afterward. Lydia was a merchant who opened her home to believers. Joseph of Arimathea was wealthy and honored Jesus in His burial.
The problem is not possessing resources.

The problem begins when resources become the measure of righteousness, when material success is presented as the normal and guaranteed outcome of sufficient faith, and when giving money is portrayed as a reliable spiritual mechanism for obtaining wealth, healing, or personal success.
That is the crucial distinction.
Biblical Christianity teaches that God is a generous Father who provides for His people according to His wisdom.

Prosperity theology, in its more extreme forms, teaches that believers can expect or claim material abundance and physical health as guaranteed benefits of faith, sometimes activated through positive declarations or financial giving.
Those are not identical messages.
One trusts God's character.
The other risks treating God's promises as a system that produces predictable material results.
And there is a devastating difference between trusting God for provision and demanding that God provide according to our expectations.
Consider one of the most frequently quoted passages in discussions about prosperity.
Third John, verse 2.
In the King James Version, the apostle writes:
At first glance, it sounds like a sweeping divine promise of wealth and health.
But look closer.
The Greek begins:
Ἀγαπητέ, περὶ πάντων εὔχομαί σε εὐοδοῦσθαι καὶ ὑγιαίνειν
Agapēte, peri pantōn euchomai se euodousthai kai hygiainein.
A careful translation is:
"Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health."
The verb εὔχομαι (euchomai) expresses a wish or prayer.
And εὐοδοῦσθαι (euodousthai) conveys the idea of things going well or succeeding.
This is a personal greeting from John to Gaius, a beloved Christian whose faithfulness and hospitality are commended in the letter.
It is not a universal guarantee that every Christian who possesses enough faith will become wealthy.
It is a prayer.
A beautiful prayer.
But a prayer is not automatically an unconditional promise.
And when we turn a personal apostolic greeting into a guaranteed financial formula, we have moved beyond what the text actually says.
Now consider another passage.
Jeremiah 29:11.
The verse has comforted countless believers, and rightly so when understood within its biblical setting.
God speaks of His plans for the welfare and future of His people.
The Hebrew includes the words:
מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה
Machshevot shalom velo lera'ah.
Meaning:
"Plans for peace/well-being and not for harm."
The word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) carries the rich sense of peace, wholeness, and well-being.
But who originally received this promise?
Jewish exiles living in Babylon.
And what did God tell them immediately before this?
That their exile would last seventy years.
Seventy years.
Imagine hearing that God's good plan included decades of waiting in a foreign land.
Imagine realizing that some who first heard the promise might never personally witness the full restoration of their nation.
Yet God remained faithful.
His promise was not false because the fulfillment did not arrive immediately.
His goodness was not absent because His people were experiencing hardship.

Jeremiah 29:11 reveals God's faithfulness to His covenant purposes in a specific historical situation. Christians may draw comfort from God's character and His ultimate redemptive purposes, but the verse does not promise every individual immediate prosperity, a successful business, or freedom from suffering.
Sometimes the most dangerous misuse of Scripture is not an outright denial of God's Word.
It is taking something God truly said and making it mean something He never intended.
And nowhere is that more apparent than in the way some people handle the words of Jesus about giving.
Luke 6:38 is often quoted:
"Give, and it shall be given unto you."
The verse continues with the picture of a generous measure being poured into one's lap.
But read the surrounding verses.
Jesus is teaching about mercy, forgiveness, generosity, and the way His disciples treat others.
He commands His followers to love their enemies, refuse vindictiveness, forgive, and give generously.
The passage is not a fundraising formula promising that a financial donation will generate a predetermined monetary return.
Jesus is forming a people who reflect the generosity of their heavenly Father.
The difference matters.
One message says, "Give because God has been generous to you."
The distorted version says, "Give because this is how you make God enrich you."
One produces worship.
The other can produce spiritualized greed.
And greed does not become holy simply because someone places a Bible verse beside it.
Now someone may ask, "But doesn't the Bible teach sowing and reaping?"
Absolutely.
Second Corinthians 9:6 teaches that whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, while whoever sows generously will also reap generously.
But Paul continues.
He says each person should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Then Paul explains that God's provision enables believers to abound in good works, increases the harvest of righteousness, and produces thanksgiving to God.
The entire discussion concerns generosity, God's sufficiency, and the needs of His people.
It is not a guarantee that every monetary gift will return as a larger cash payment.
In fact, Paul's emphasis is profoundly different.
God enriches His people in ways that equip them for generosity.
He does not instruct them to use generosity as a technique for enriching themselves.
And here is a question worth asking.
If someone gives only because they have been promised more money in return, is that truly the selfless generosity Jesus taught?
Or has giving quietly become an investment strategy dressed in religious language?
This is why motive matters.
This is why context matters.
And this is why those who teach Scripture carry such serious responsibility.
But perhaps the most revealing passage of all comes from the apostle Paul himself.
In Philippians 4:12–13, Paul explains that he knows what it means to have little and what it means to have plenty.
He has learned the secret of facing hunger and abundance, need and provision.
Then he declares:
"I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me."
How often have we heard that verse used as a promise that Christians can achieve any ambition?
A bigger house.
A successful business.
A dream career.
Financial independence.
Yet Paul was not writing from a luxury residence while celebrating his latest breakthrough.
He was writing as a man acquainted with imprisonment, hardship, and dependence upon Christ.
The Greek expression in Philippians 4:13 is:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.
A faithful rendering is:
"I have strength for all things through the one who strengthens me."
In context, those "all things" refer to the circumstances Paul has just described, including both plenty and hunger.
Paul was not claiming that Christ guaranteed him unlimited achievement.
He was declaring that Christ strengthened him to remain faithful regardless of his circumstances.
Read that again.
The promise was not that Paul would never experience lack. The promise was that Christ would sustain him even when he did.
That is not a smaller Gospel.
That is a deeper one.
Because a faith that survives only when the bank account is full has not yet learned the secret Paul was describing.
A faith that worships only when the diagnosis is favorable is vulnerable to collapse when suffering arrives.
But a faith anchored in the crucified and risen Christ can say through tears, "Lord, I do not understand what is happening, but I still belong to You."
And this brings us to a man whose life should make every prosperity preacher reconsider any promise of guaranteed comfort.
Jesus Christ Himself.
The Son of God entered the world in humility.
He lived without the kind of earthly security that many people today associate with divine favor.
In Luke 9:58, Jesus said that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.
He was rejected.
Misunderstood.
Betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
And crucified.
Now ask yourself something.
If material prosperity is the necessary evidence of God's approval, what do we do with the earthly life of Jesus?
If suffering always proves a lack of faith, what do we do with Gethsemane?
If opposition means someone has failed to activate divine favor, what do we do with Calvary?
And if God's greatest blessing must look like visible success, how do we explain the cross?
The cross looked like defeat.
The crowd mocked.
The disciples scattered.
The religious leaders believed they had won.
But what looked like humiliation became the place where God's redemptive purpose was accomplished.
Jesus bore our sins.
He suffered in our place.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, sinners are offered forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
The center of Christianity is not a promise that believers will never experience suffering.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death, and that everyone who turns to Him in faith receives a treasure this world cannot manufacture or destroy.
That is the Gospel.
And no earthly prosperity can compare with it.
The apostle Paul understood this.
In Second Corinthians 12, he describes a painful affliction he calls a thorn in the flesh.
Three times he pleaded with the Lord to remove it.
Three times.
This was not a spiritually immature believer who had forgotten how to pray.
This was an apostle of Jesus Christ.
A man who had seen extraordinary revelations.
A man through whom God had performed remarkable works.
Yet the affliction remained.
And God's answer was not, "Paul, your faith is too weak."
It was:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
Second Corinthians 12:9.
Those words should change how we speak to suffering Christians.
Because sometimes God delivers His people from suffering.
And sometimes He sustains them through it.
Both can display His faithfulness.
Neither gives us permission to condemn a suffering believer as spiritually defective.
Think of the Christian mother who prays for healing but still has to attend chemotherapy.
Think of the father who faithfully gives to his church yet struggles to buy groceries.
Think of the elderly widow who loves Jesus deeply but lives on a small pension.
Think of believers in places where following Christ may cost them employment, freedom, or even their lives.
Are we prepared to tell them that their hardships prove they have not believed enough?
Are we prepared to say that persecuted Christians are missing the blessings of God because they have not discovered the right financial principles?
Or might it be that the Church has sometimes confused the comforts of a prosperous society with the promises of the eternal Kingdom?
Hebrews 11 gives us a startling answer.
The chapter celebrates people who conquered kingdoms, escaped danger, and witnessed extraordinary deliverance through faith.
But then the narrative changes.
Others were tortured.
Some suffered mockery, imprisonment, and violence.
Others wandered in poverty and affliction.
And Scripture says that the world was not worthy of them.
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not divide the faithful into those who believed enough to become prosperous and those who failed.
It presents both deliverance and suffering within the testimony of faith.
Some believers escaped the sword.
Others died by it.
And both could belong to God.
That truth is not comfortable.
But it is liberating.
Because it means your circumstances do not have the final authority to define your relationship with Jesus.
Your financial situation is not your spiritual identity.
Your medical condition is not a verdict on your worth before God.
Your unanswered prayer is not proof that Christ has abandoned you.
And your suffering does not cancel the promises of the resurrection.
Now, does that mean Christians should never pray for prosperity, provision, or healing?
No.
Jesus taught His disciples to ask the Father for daily bread.
James instructed the sick to seek prayer.
Paul encouraged believers to work, share, and care for those in need.
Scripture celebrates honest labor, wise stewardship, generosity, and gratitude for God's gifts.
There is nothing inherently unspiritual about asking God to provide a job, restore health, rescue a family from debt, or bless a business.
The difference lies in whether we approach God as our Father or attempt to control Him through a formula.
A child can ask a loving father for help without believing that the father is obligated to grant every request exactly as desired.
Prayer is an expression of dependence.
It is not a contract that places God under our command.
And genuine faith does not mean believing that we can dictate the outcome.
It means trusting the Lord whose wisdom exceeds our own.
But now we must confront something even more uncomfortable.
Because the danger of prosperity theology does not end with misunderstood Bible verses.
Sometimes it becomes a system of spiritual pressure.
A struggling believer hears that a special offering will unlock a miracle.
A desperate parent is encouraged to give beyond their means to demonstrate faith.
A person awaiting medical results is told that a financial seed will release supernatural healing.
And when the promised result fails to arrive, the explanation shifts.
Perhaps the person doubted.
Perhaps they spoke negatively.
Perhaps they failed to give enough.
The burden returns to the wounded believer.
That is not how shepherds are called to care for Christ's flock.
First Peter 5:2–3 instructs elders to shepherd God's people willingly and not for shameful gain or through domineering leadership.
And First Timothy 6 speaks with extraordinary clarity.
Paul warns about people who imagine that godliness is a means of financial gain.
Then he writes:
First Timothy 6:6.
The Greek phrase is:
ἔστιν δὲ πορισμὸς μέγας ἡ εὐσέβεια μετὰ αὐταρκείας
Estin de porismos megas hē eusebeia meta autarkeias.
Meaning:
"Godliness with contentment is great gain."
The word αὐτάρκεια (autarkeia) refers to contentment or sufficiency.
And the irony is powerful.
Paul uses the language of gain to redefine what true gain looks like.
Not godliness as a tool for accumulating wealth.
Godliness accompanied by contentment.
He continues by warning that those who desire to be rich can fall into temptation and destructive desires.
He does not say money itself is the root of every evil.
He warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
That distinction matters.
Wealth is not automatically wicked.
Poverty is not automatically holy.
But the craving for wealth can become an idol, and religious language does not make that craving harmless.
In Matthew 6:24, Jesus declared that no one can serve two masters.
He specifically named God and mammon, a term referring to wealth or riches.
He did not merely warn that money might become distracting.
He described a conflict of allegiance.
And perhaps that is where this discussion becomes painfully personal.
Because it is easy to criticize a preacher who promises luxury cars and enormous houses.
It is harder to recognize the same desire in our own hearts.
Have we ever treated prayer as a way of getting what we want rather than drawing near to God?
Have we ever measured God's love by whether life was going well?
Have we ever felt more grateful for the blessing than for the One who gave it?
Have we ever wanted Jesus to improve our circumstances while resisting His authority over our lives?
The prosperity gospel is not merely a problem somewhere on a television screen.
Its underlying temptation can whisper inside any human heart.
I will follow You, Lord, as long as You make my life work.
I will trust You, as long as You protect everything I love.
I will obey You, as long as obedience brings visible rewards.
And then Jesus speaks words that cut through every condition we try to attach to discipleship.
In Luke 9:23, He says that anyone who would follow Him must deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Him.
Not take up his guaranteed financial breakthrough.
Not take up his promise of an effortless life.
His cross.
The cross represents surrender.
It represents dying to the illusion that we belong to ourselves.
It represents following Jesus even when obedience is costly.
And that is where the prosperity gospel, when preached as a guarantee of earthly success, collides with the teachings of Christ.
Because Jesus never concealed the cost of following Him.
He told His disciples that they would face trouble.
He warned that the world would hate them.
He called them to seek first God's Kingdom and righteousness.
He taught them to store up treasures in heaven.
And He promised something infinitely greater than uninterrupted earthly comfort.
He promised Himself.
Now we can answer the question we began with.
Is the prosperity gospel simply a misunderstanding of Scripture, or is it a different gospel altogether?
The answer requires both discernment and precision.

Some prosperity-oriented teachings arise from sincere but mistaken interpretations of biblical passages. A believer may genuinely love Jesus while misunderstanding texts about blessing, healing, giving, or provision.
Such errors should be corrected patiently, carefully, and biblically.

But when a message systematically replaces repentance with self-improvement, substitutes guaranteed wealth for the hope of eternal life, treats financial giving as a mechanism for purchasing divine favor, or makes material success the central proof of saving faith, the problem becomes far more serious.
At that point, we are not merely dealing with an overemphasis on blessing.
We are confronting a distortion of the Gospel's center.

And if the message of Christ crucified and risen is displaced by a message that fundamentally makes God the means to our material ambitions, then the warning about a different gospel becomes profoundly relevant.
We should not claim to know every preacher's motives or every listener's spiritual condition.
But we must examine what is actually being taught.
Because sincerity does not make a false promise true.
Popularity does not establish biblical authority.
And a crowded church does not automatically prove that its message faithfully represents Jesus.
The Gospel must be tested by Scripture, not by applause.
And here is the part that may surprise you.
The answer to prosperity theology is not a gospel of misery.
It is not teaching that God enjoys watching His children suffer.
It is not glorifying poverty or telling believers to refuse every earthly blessing.
It is recovering the incomparable riches of Christ.
In Ephesians 1:3, Paul praises God for blessing believers in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
He then speaks of election in Christ, adoption, redemption through His blood, forgiveness of sins, and the riches of divine grace.
These blessings are not imaginary.
They are not consolation prizes for people who failed to become wealthy.
They are the deepest realities of Christian salvation.
A person can own a mansion and still be spiritually lost.
Another can live in a small rented room and possess eternal life in Christ.
A person can have perfect health and remain unreconciled to God.
Another can be physically weak yet belong forever to the risen Savior.
The question is not whether you have enough money to be considered blessed.
The question is whether you have been reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Because if you gain the whole world and lose your soul, you have gained nothing that can save you.
But if you belong to Christ, then even death cannot separate you from His love.
Romans 8:35–39 makes that truth unmistakable.
Tribulation cannot separate us from Christ.
Distress cannot separate us.
Persecution cannot separate us.
Famine cannot separate us.
Nakedness, danger, and the sword cannot separate us.
Notice something extraordinary.
Paul does not say these things will never happen to believers.
He says they cannot separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
That is a promise strong enough to carry a suffering Christian through the darkest night.
And it is a promise no prosperity formula can improve.
Maybe you are reading this while facing financial hardship.
Maybe you once believed that a certain offering would change your circumstances.
Maybe you gave sincerely, prayed desperately, and waited for a miracle that never came.
Maybe someone told you that your suffering was evidence of weak faith.
And perhaps, after enough disappointment, you quietly stopped praying.
Not because you stopped wanting God.
But because you began wondering whether God wanted you.
Hear what Scripture actually teaches.
The Father does not sell His love.
Christ does not auction His mercy.
The Holy Spirit is not a reward purchased by the highest donor.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And God's grace cannot be purchased through an offering.
You do not have to make yourself wealthy enough, successful enough, or impressive enough to come to Jesus.
Come with your sins.
Come with your doubts.
Come with your disappointments.
Come with your repentance.
Come with the truth about who you are.
Jesus did not die to make you a more successful consumer.
He died to redeem sinners and bring them to God.
And the resurrection announces that sin and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is where the story turns.
The scandal of human greed, religious exploitation, misplaced trust, and our desperate attempts to control God meets the astonishing grace of a Savior who gives Himself freely.
And perhaps the greatest miracle you need today is not the sudden arrival of wealth.
Perhaps it is the restoration of your confidence in the Jesus who was always enough, even when life was not.
Not because your needs are insignificant.
They matter deeply.
Not because God is indifferent to your pain.
He invites you to bring your burdens to Him.
But because the greatest gift of the Gospel is not something Christ places in your hands.
It is Christ Himself.
And when you finally see that, something changes.
You can work diligently without worshiping success.
You can enjoy blessings without building your identity upon them.
You can give generously without trying to purchase a miracle.
You can pray boldly while surrendering the outcome to your Father's wisdom.
You can grieve without concluding that God has abandoned you.
And you can rejoice in Christ even when the world gives you little reason to celebrate.
That is not defeat.
That is freedom.
And it is the kind of freedom the Church desperately needs to recover.
There is another responsibility that comes with this truth.
Those of us who teach, write, preach, publish, or share Christian content must be willing to apply these same principles to ourselves.
But it must remain voluntary, transparent, and free from spiritual coercion.
Paul himself thanked the Philippian believers for supporting his ministry, describing their generosity as participation in his work and as an offering pleasing to God (Philippians 4:10–18).
Their giving mattered.
It helped sustain Gospel ministry.
But Paul's confidence was ultimately in Christ, not in the size of their gifts.

If these articles have helped you understand Scripture more faithfully, return to Jesus more deeply, or recognize teachings that once confused you, I invite you to become part of the work that makes this ministry possible.
It can be a voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in ministry, much like the support believers offered to those serving the early Church.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and the faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
But because Gospel work requires people willing to serve, give, teach, and share.
That benefit is simply our way of saying thank you.
It is not a spiritual reward, and it does not measure anyone's standing before God.
Your worth to Christ has never depended on your financial capacity.
You are welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep growing.
And please keep testing everything, including what we publish, against the Word of God.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that depends unquestioningly on Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus Christ and help them become rooted in Scripture, faithful in discipleship, and discerning in a world filled with competing messages.
And sometimes the simplest way to participate in that mission costs nothing.
Not merely to increase a page's reach, but because someone in your circle may be carrying guilt from a religious promise that never came true.
Someone may have been told that poverty proves God's displeasure.
Someone may be grieving an unanswered prayer.
Someone may have walked away from church because they were promised a version of Christianity that collapsed under the weight of real suffering.
And perhaps a careful, compassionate explanation of Scripture could help that person see Jesus clearly again.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, spiritual seekers, and even those who no longer believe to follow along.
There is room for honest questions here.
There is room for people who have been hurt.
There is room for those who are learning how to distinguish the voice of Christ from the promises people have made in His name.
And I want to ask you something personally.
Not as a test of your spirituality.
Not as a way to measure your faith.
But because your experience may help someone else feel less alone.
Have you ever been made to feel that God was disappointed in you because you were struggling financially, physically, or emotionally?
Or have you ever confused God's blessing with material success, only to discover through hardship that His grace was greater than you understood?
You can simply comment, "Jesus, teach me to treasure You above everything."
Or comment, "Christ is still healing me," if you are recovering from spiritual disappointment.
And if your faith has been exhausted lately, you can comment, "Pray for me."
You do not need to share details you would rather keep private.
But your honest testimony might become the encouragement another person needs.
Because this is not just a debate about theology.
This is about the woman who thinks God rejected her because her prayers for healing were not answered as she expected.
This is about the father who believes he has failed spiritually because he cannot provide everything his children need.
This is about the young believer who gave money he could not afford because someone promised him a miracle.
This is about the person who has quietly wondered whether Christianity itself was false, when what failed was a human promise that Scripture never made.
And this is about the Church remembering the Savior at the center of everything.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for our sins.
Risen from the dead.
Calling sinners to repentance.
Offering forgiveness through grace.
Giving eternal life to those who trust in Him.
The Gospel does not promise that following Jesus will make every chapter of your earthly life comfortable.
It promises that those who belong to Him have a living hope that reaches beyond suffering, beyond poverty, beyond sickness, and even beyond the grave.
And when the final chapter comes, the Christian's greatest joy will not be discovering how much wealth was accumulated on earth.
It will be seeing the Savior whose grace was sufficient all along.
So pray for provision.
Work faithfully.
Give generously.
Receive God's blessings with gratitude.
Seek healing.
Care for the poor.
Support faithful Gospel ministry as you are able.
And never apologize for thanking God when He answers your prayers in wonderful and unexpected ways.
But do not allow anyone to convince you that Jesus is valuable only because of what He can give you.
He is worthy when the harvest is abundant.
He is worthy when the fields are empty.
He is worthy when healing comes.
He is worthy when the struggle continues.
He is worthy when the door opens.
He is worthy when you must wait.
And He is worthy because He is the crucified and risen Lord, not because He has agreed to fulfill every earthly dream.
The prosperity gospel, at its most distorted, asks what you can gain by having Jesus.
The true Gospel announces what God has already given through Jesus—and calls you to surrender your life to Him.
And that changes everything.
You may have lost the prosperity you were promised, but in Jesus Christ you can discover the grace you were never able to buy.
